title: Download & Install
lede: Two ways in: write a ready-made image to a card, or download the build for your machine and run a couple of commands. After that, add only the extras you actually want. Polaris looks around at startup and simply hides what is not there, so nothing nags you to install something you do not need.

requirements.title: System requirements
requirements.sub: RAM is what really decides. Everything else is comfortable on any modern little board, and a few of them even lend a GPU or an NPU to the AI tools.
requirements.ramNote: Polaris sizes the live stack to the board it is running on, picking full, half or quarter resolution so the work fits in a quarter of the memory. In round numbers: a 12 MP colour camera needs about 900 MB at full resolution and 450 MB at half, on top of a fixed 370 MB for everything else. 2 GB is comfortable, a 1.5 GB board works at reduced resolution, and if you would rather not spend the memory at all, the browser can do the stacking instead.
requirements.recommendedNote: Recommended board: the Orange Pi 4 Pro with 4 GB. It is the best balance of cost and capability of every SBC tested so far: a Polaris score of 180 for around $50 to $70, with eight cores, LPDDR5 memory, a GPU and a 3 TOPS NPU. If you want the highest score whatever the price, the Radxa Dragon Q6A leads at 317. If you lean on the AI tools, the Orange Pi 5 Pro is the proven accelerated option, adding OpenCL on the GPU and GraXpert AI on the NPU.

rows.notes: Broadcom BCM2837 (4x Cortex-A53, up to 1.2 GHz), VideoCore IV GPU. Runs, but tight; PHD2 GUI embed is auto-disabled (32-bit ARM gate).

Broadcom BCM2711 (4x Cortex-A72, up to 1.8 GHz), VideoCore VI GPU, LPDDR4. Comfortable at 2 GB: the live stack drops to a lower stacking resolution on its own, and client-side WASM can offload the heavy math.
Broadcom BCM2712 (4x Cortex-A76, up to 2.4 GHz), VideoCore VII GPU, LPDDR4X. Lossless: live stacking plus simultaneous Studio jobs are fine.

The best balance of cost and capability here: Polaris score 180, at the price of a Raspberry Pi 4. Allwinner A733 (2x Cortex-A76 + 6x Cortex-A55, up to 2.0 GHz), Imagination BXM-4-64 GPU, 3 TOPS NPU, LPDDR5. Active cooling is worth it: it holds the CPU clocks up under the sustained load. Same GPU-plus-NPU story as the 5 Pro (OpenCL on the GPU, GraXpert on the NPU), pending validation.
Proven daily driver, and the pick if you want AI acceleration. RK3588S (4x Cortex-A76 + 4x Cortex-A55), Mali-G610 GPU, 6 TOPS NPU. Full experience: OpenCL on the GPU and GraXpert AI on the NPU.

The fastest SBC tested so far (Polaris score 317), on the strength of its CPU. Qualcomm QCS6490 (octa-core Kryo: 1x 2.7 GHz + 3x 2.4 GHz + 4x 1.9 GHz), LPDDR5. Polaris runs the image pipeline CPU-only here: the Adreno GPU is a net loss, so the OpenCL toggle stays off. The Hexagon NPU is used, through QAIRT, for the AI tools.
Same feature set as Linux, plus vendor DSLR drivers.

images.title: Ready-to-flash images
images.sub: The quickest way to start: pick your board below, write the image to a card, and turn it on. Polaris is already installed and set up, there is nothing to configure. Write the image with Raspberry Pi Imager, balenaEtcher or Rufus. The files live on Google Drive, and a new board appears here once it has been tested.
images.bootNote: Turn the board on and it just works. Polaris starts by itself: no setup, no account, nothing to install. If the board has WiFi and does not recognise any network around it, it creates one of its own, called Polaris-Hotspot (the password is polaris1234). Connect your phone or laptop to that network and open Polaris in the browser.

tips.body:
How do I open Polaris? The same way you open a website: by typing an address in any browser.
The address is your board's number. Open your router's page or app and look at the list of connected devices (often called DHCP or Clients). Your board is in there, with a number like 192.168.1.42. Type https://192.168.1.42:5000 in the browser, using your own number.
A shortcut: on Raspberry Pi you can type the name instead, like https://polaris-pi.local:5000. Some Orange Pi images cannot do that, so there use the number.
The browser will warn you about the certificate. That is expected and it is not a problem: the board signs its own, because it lives on your home network and not on the internet. Accept it once and it stops asking.
Cannot find the board? It has probably not joined your WiFi yet, so it is still offering its own Polaris-Hotspot. Connect to that hotspot (or plug in a network cable), then set your WiFi in Settings, Network.

The update button does not work? On a few of the older images the one-click update stops with a permission error. Nothing is broken and nothing of yours is lost: that image simply shipped with a rule its system ignores. You can update by hand instead. Connect with ssh polaris@192.168.1.42 (your board's number), then run wget https://github.com/DanWBR/NINA.Polaris/releases/latest/download/polaris_arm64.deb and sudo apt install ./polaris_arm64.deb. Your profiles, photos and settings all stay where they are.

items.note: For any 64-bit PC or mini PC. 7-Zip archive: extract, write the .img to a USB stick with balenaEtcher or Rufus, and boot from it. To move Polaris onto the machine's internal SSD, boot the stick and run sudo polaris-install-to-disk: it clones the running system to the disk you pick and makes it bootable, so you never have to write the image to a disk you cannot boot from.

Entry-level 1.5 GB board. HDD Raw Copy Tool image (imgcv2): extract the .7z, then write the .img to an SD card with HDD Raw Copy Tool (or balenaEtcher / Rufus). Login password: polaris1234. GPU acceleration stays off here (the Mali-G31 is a net loss on this pipeline).

Recommended board: the best balance of cost and capability. Shrunk raw image. 7-Zip archive: extract the .7z, then write the .img to the internal storage with HDD Raw Copy Tool (or balenaEtcher / Rufus). Login password: polaris1234.

update.title: Keeping Polaris up to date
update.selfBody: Every .deb install, including the ready-to-flash images above, can update itself. Polaris checks GitHub for new releases when it starts and once an hour after that. When there is a newer build for your board, a green Update badge shows up in the top bar with the version number. Click it to read what changed, then Download and install: Polaris fetches the right file, installs it and comes back on the new version. No SSH, no apt, no sudo password. Just leave the page open while it reloads itself. Your profiles and your photos stay exactly where they are.

download.title: Download
download.sub: Pick the server build for the machine that will sit next to the telescope, then follow the steps below. Want zero setup? Take a ready-to-flash image above instead.

groups.name: Server (runs on the rig)
groups.note: Install on the Raspberry Pi, SBC, or mini PC that controls your gear.

groups.name: Client apps (connect from a device)
groups.note: Optional native app to reach the server. Any browser also works, so no app is required.

tldr.title: Bare minimum to boot
tldr.note: That is everything the home page needs. Each of the other features brings its own tool, listed under optional components below, and you add them only when you want that feature.

rows.label: Runtime
rows.windows: .NET 10 Desktop Runtime (bundled in the self-contained build)
rows.linux: .NET 10 Runtime, or use the self-contained build

platformsSection.title: Install
platformsSection.sub: Once you have the files, here is the step by step for each platform. The published builds carry everything they need, so there is no runtime to chase.

platforms.name: Raspberry Pi & arm64 SBCs
platforms.summary: The recommended path for any Debian or Ubuntu arm64 board: Raspberry Pi, Orange Pi, Radxa, and similar. The .deb creates the user, a systemd unit, the indi-web venv, apt dependencies, and a self-signed HTTPS cert.
platforms.notes: Running at https://<hostname>.local:5000 in about 30 seconds. Manage it with: sudo systemctl status polaris, sudo journalctl -u polaris -f, sudo systemctl restart polaris.

platforms.name: Mini PC, full stack (recommended)
platforms.summary: Install Ubuntu with its own installer (it partitions the SSD properly and uses all of it), then run one command. This adds everything the ready-to-flash image has and the .deb alone does not: INDI with third-party drivers, PHD2, astrometry.net, ASTAP with the d80 database, and Polaris itself. It is the very script the image is built from, so the two cannot drift apart.
platforms.notes: No 13 GB image to write to an internal disk. Add --addon to install the software on a machine you already use, without creating the polaris user, autologin, hostname or sleep policy.

platforms.name: x86-64 PC (Debian / Ubuntu)
platforms.summary: The same one-command install for any 64-bit Intel or AMD PC or mini PC running Debian or Ubuntu. Sets up the user, systemd unit, indi-web, dependencies, and HTTPS cert, exactly like the SBC build.
platforms.notes: Running at https://<hostname>.local:5000 in about 30 seconds, managed by systemd; same status, journalctl, and restart commands as the arm64 build.

platforms.name: Other Linux (portable)
platforms.summary: For Fedora, Arch, or any non-Debian distro, or when you prefer no systemd integration. Replace linux-arm64 with linux-x64 for Intel/AMD.
platforms.notes: Runs in the foreground. Wire your own service unit if you want it to survive reboots.

platforms.name: Windows mini PC
platforms.summary: Portable, no installer. ARM64 build also available (polaris-win-arm64.zip) for Surface Pro X and some Copilot+ PCs.
platforms.steps:
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri "https://github.com/DanWBR/NINA.Polaris/releases/latest/download/polaris-win-x64.zip" -OutFile polaris.zip
Expand-Archive polaris.zip
cd polaris-win-x64
.\NINA.Polaris.exe
platforms.notes: Open https://localhost:5000 and accept the self-signed cert once. Remember to open the firewall (see below).

platforms.name: Docker
platforms.summary: Multi-arch image (arm64 + amd64). The compose file in the repo includes indiserver in the same stack.
platforms.notes: Volumes mount /config (profiles) and /images (FITS output). On Linux use --network host, or port-forward TCP 5000 and UDP 5353 in compose.

platforms.name: Build from source
platforms.summary: For developers or unsupported platforms. Needs the .NET 10 SDK and Git (with submodules).
platforms.steps:
git clone https://github.com/DanWBR/NINA.Polaris.git
cd NINA.Polaris
./deploy/publish-linux-arm64.sh   # or publish-linux-x64.sh / publish-win-x64.ps1
./publish/linux-arm64/NINA.Polaris
platforms.notes: Build and test target net10.0. The stellarium-web submodule ships pinned .js/.wasm, so Emscripten is only needed if you bump the engine.

firewall.title: Open the firewall
firewall.sub: Polaris listens on TCP 5000 (the interface) and UDP 5353 (mDNS, which is what makes the <hostname>.local address work). Most systems block both until you say otherwise.
firewall.windows:
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Polaris Astro Controller" -Direction Inbound -Protocol TCP -LocalPort 5000 -Action Allow -Profile Private,Domain
New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "mDNS (Polaris)" -Direction Inbound -Protocol UDP -LocalPort 5353 -Action Allow -Profile Private,Domain
firewall.linux:
sudo ufw allow 5000/tcp
sudo ufw allow 5353/udp
firewall.note: On Linux without ufw: iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 5000 -j ACCEPT. The .deb install handles this for you.

optionalSection.title: Optional components
optionalSection.sub: Add only what you need. Each feature lights up when its tool is there, and stays quietly out of the way when it is not.

optionalGroups.name: Equipment drivers
optionalGroups.intro: At least one bus is required to control hardware. Both can coexist; the active rig stores a per-device driver choice.

items.name: INDI
items.purpose: Preferred on Linux. The indi-full meta-package ships the daemon plus 100+ drivers (ZWO, Canon, EQMod, Celestron, weather, ...).
items.windows: Runs via WSL2 or a windi build; most Windows users pick Alpaca instead.

items.name: ASCOM / Alpaca
items.purpose: Preferred on Windows. Polaris discovers Alpaca devices over the LAN via UDP.
items.windows: ASCOM Platform 7+ (free) + the driver pack per device. Alpaca on by default.
items.linux: Run an Alpaca-compatible device server; most modern drivers expose Alpaca natively.

items.name: Vendor SDKs (DSLR / mirrorless)
items.purpose: Canon, Nikon, and Sony DSLR/mirrorless on Windows. Drop the DLLs into plugins/ after registering with the vendor (EULA blocks redistribution).
items.windows: Canon EDSDK 13.x+ in plugins/canon-edsdk/, Nikon SDK in plugins/nikon-sdk/, Sony SDK in plugins/sony-sdk/.
items.linux: Not needed: DSLRs use indi_gphoto_ccd from indi-full.

optionalGroups.name: Plate solving
optionalGroups.intro: Required for Slew & Center (the centering loop). Without any solver, Slew Only still slews the mount. Polaris dispatches primary then blind fallback across whatever is installed.

items.name: ASTAP
items.purpose: Default solver. Fast (about 1 to 3 s), works offline, MIT. Recommended for everyone.
items.windows: astap.exe installer + the H17/H18 star database (~2 GB).

items.name: PlateSolve3
items.purpose: Faster than ASTAP at long focal lengths. Free for non-commercial use.

items.name: Astrometry.net (local)
items.purpose: The gold standard, but slow on a Pi (about 30 to 60 s).
items.linux: sudo apt install astrometry.net + index files.

items.name: Astrometry.net (online)
items.purpose: Last resort. About 30 to 60 s per solve, free with an API key.

optionalGroups.name: Autoguiding
optionalGroups.intro: Polaris guides out of the box with a built-in, native PHD2, so there is nothing to install for basic guiding.

items.name: PHD2 (optional, the original app)
items.purpose: Prefer the real PHD2 over the native implementation? Install it on Windows or Linux, and Polaris drives it from inside the browser through an embedded remote view, no second screen needed. It still auto-detects PHD2, swaps profiles, runs Smart Calibrate, and broadcasts guide stats in real time.

items.name: Embedded remote view
items.purpose: Shows the installed PHD2 inside the Polaris GUIDE tab over a remote connection, no extra screen. Not supported on 32-bit Raspberry Pi (auto-gated).
items.windows: TightVNC, which Polaris bridges into the browser via noVNC.

optionalGroups.name: Post-processing
optionalGroups.intro: Detected at startup via the binary locator. Polaris grays out the matching STUDIO buttons when missing.

items.name: Siril
items.purpose: Replaces the built-in stacking pipeline in STUDIO with Siril scripts (5 bundled, plus your own ~/.siril/scripts).

items.name: GraXpert
items.purpose: Background extraction (auto per-frame during sequences if toggled), plus deconvolution and denoise on v3.0+.
items.linux: AppImage from the GraXpert releases page.

optionalGroups.name: Simulators (no hardware)
optionalGroups.intro: Test the whole pipeline without a scope. Settings then Equipment simulator detects the install and spawns the stack with one click.

items.name: INDI simulators
items.purpose: Renders real stars from the GSC catalog at the simulated mount position.
items.windows: Use the Alpaca Omni Simulator instead.

items.name: Alpaca Omni Simulator
items.purpose: A single .exe exposing the ASCOM Camera/Telescope/Focuser/FilterWheel simulators over Alpaca.
items.windows: Download and run the Omni Simulator.

items.name: Relay server (remote internet access)
items.purpose: Reach your rig from anywhere without exposing it directly. Reverse-tunnels over HTTPS with per-tenant tokens, mTLS, quotas, and built-in Let's Encrypt.
items.windows: Host NINA.Relay.Server on a public VPS (Linux). The rig side needs nothing extra.
items.linux: Run the Linux x64/arm64 build on a VPS with a domain and ports 80/443 open.

items.name: Remote terminal
items.purpose: Browser-based SSH from the Polaris tab to restart services on a headless host. Set Terminal:Enabled = true in appsettings.json.
items.linux: sudo apt install openssh-server (already present on Raspberry Pi OS).

items.name: Stellarium sync
items.purpose: Pull the currently selected object from Stellarium into the SKY tab as a target.
items.windows: Enable Plugins then Remote Control, bind to 127.0.0.1:8090.
items.linux: Same: enable the Remote Control plugin on 127.0.0.1:8090.
